**Why this matters:** the session gave you the main ideas of data management and publishing. This reading holds the
detail you'll want when you actually write a data management plan or publish a dataset: what a plan covers, each
FAIR letter at the moment of publishing, how two water repositories compare, and how data and code get peer
reviewed. About 15 minutes.

## What a data management plan covers

Many funders now require a data management plan (DMP) or data management and sharing plan (DMSP) as part of a
proposal. While the specifics differ by agency and program, most ask you to address a similar set of questions
([Wong, 2026](https://www.cuahsi.org/uploads/pages/doc/DMP_guide_digital.pdf)):

| A DMP or DMSP often provides answers to... | What that can look like in a water project |
| --- | --- |
| What data will you create or collect? | Continuous sensor records, grab samples, field notes, model output |
| What formats and standards will you use? | CSV for tabular data, standard units and variable codes (for example, USGS parameter codes), a documented file naming scheme |
| How will you document and describe the data? | A data dictionary, site metadata table, and a README |
| Where will data be stored and backed up during the project? | A project folder with a single source of truth, version-controlled code, and a backup plan |
| How will data be shared and preserved? | A data repository such as HydroShare, with a DOI |
| Who is responsible for what? | Named people for QA/QC, data release, and updates |
| Are there access, privacy, or licensing considerations? | Sensitive locations, data-sharing agreements, an open license for what *can* be shared |

A few tips that make a plan more useful than a box to check:

- **Treat it as a living document.** Projects change. Revisit your plan when your sensors, collaborators, or
  questions change.
- **Plan for the sharing step early.** Choosing a repository and a license at the *start* of a project means you can
  organize and document with the end in mind.
- **Use existing tools and resources.** Many university library and research offices offer their own data
  management plan tools, templates, and one-on-one support.

## Reproducibility: the definitions in full

The National Academies define reproducibility as obtaining consistent computational results using the same input
data, code, methods, and conditions of analysis, and replicability as obtaining consistent results across studies
that ask the same question, each with its own data ([NASEM, 2019](https://doi.org/10.17226/25303)). The Turing Way
uses a two-by-two view: a result is reproducible when the same analysis on the same data gives the same answer,
replicable when the same analysis on different data gives qualitatively similar answers, and robust when different
analysis workflows on the same data give qualitatively similar answers
([The Turing Way Community, n.d.](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/overview/overview-definitions)).
Some fields even use the two terms the opposite way round ([Barba, 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.03311)). This
course uses a broader working definition: methods can be easily rebuilt using the same data to recreate results or
new data to update an analysis ([Platt, 2025](https://youtu.be/74GjxHnhlr0)).

## FAIR in action, letter by letter

Many repositories and services can check some FAIR criteria automatically.
[DataONE's MetaDIG engine](https://github.com/NCEAS/metadig-checks) runs a suite of open source checks, such as
whether the metadata document is valid against its schema, and sorts the results into F, A, I, and R. These scores
measure whether metadata are machine-readable, not whether the data themselves are correct, so they complement
careful documentation and human review rather than replace them.

### F = Findable

Findability starts with persistent identifiers, which link people and data indefinitely:

- **DOIs (Digital Object Identifiers)** for your dataset or software release. A DOI keeps resolving even if a
  repository redesigns its website, and it is what lets others cite your data.
- **[ORCID iDs](https://orcid.org)** for the authors. These tell people with common names apart, follow you from
  institution to institution, and connect your data, code, and papers back to you.

Whichever repository you pick, look for one that provides a DOI, descriptive metadata, and long-term preservation.

### A = Accessible

Accessible does not always mean open, but the rules for access must be explicit. Someone who lands on your record
should be able to tell whether the data are public, embargoed until a certain date, or available on request, and who
they would ask. Repositories often support embargoes, which let you get a DOI and publish descriptive metadata now and
release the files later. For instance, the EarthChem Library
[lets contributors embargo files for up to two years](https://earthchem.org/ecl/policies). Even when the data
themselves must be restricted, the metadata should remain findable.

The CARE principles ([GIDA](https://www.gida-global.org/careprinciples)) come back into play here. If your data
relate to Indigenous Peoples, lands, or waters, check the CARE principles and the terms attached to your sources
before you decide how to share. Whatever is restricted should be explained in the record.

### I = Interoperable

Interoperable data can be combined with other data and opened with many different tools, by people and by machines.
In practice this means choosing common, non-proprietary formats:

- **Tabular data:** CSV or TSV (plain-text tables with values separated by commas or tabs) rather than an Excel file
  with merged cells, color-coded meaning, or notes mixed in with the data.
- **Gridded or multidimensional data:** NetCDF, a self-describing format that stores arrays together with their
  metadata (ideally following [CF conventions](https://cfconventions.org)), or Zarr.
- **Spatial data:** GeoTIFF (an image file with its map location built in) for rasters, and GeoPackage (a
  single-file spatial database) or GeoJSON (plain-text JSON) for vector data. (If you use a shapefile, keep all of
  its component files together.)
- **Documentation:** plain text, Markdown, or PDF.

Follow the tidy data rules: one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell, with site and
variable descriptions kept in a separate metadata table. Clear, consistent file names help too:
`discharge_daily_site01_2024.csv` will mean much more to a stranger than `Q_dv_s01_24.csv`. State your units, time
zones, and coordinate reference systems in the metadata so others can combine your data with theirs.

### R = Reusable

Metadata are the who, what, when, where, why, and how of your data, and the README is the homepage of your dataset.
The ingredients are:

- **A license.** Without one, others have no clear permission to reuse your work, even if it is public.
  [CC0 or CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/) are common for data, and permissive licenses like MIT,
  BSD, or Apache 2.0 are common for code ([choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com) can help).
- **Rich metadata.** Title, abstract, authors with ORCIDs, geographic and temporal coverage, funding, and related
  publications, plus a description of each variable: its units, definition, and how it was derived.
- **A README.** Describe what each file is and how the files relate, define variables, units, and abbreviations,
  explain how the data were collected or produced (including known issues and missing-value codes), list the
  software and versions needed, and say how to cite it and who to contact.
- **Shared vocabularies.** Community conventions, like CF standard names for NetCDF variables, controlled
  vocabularies for hydrologic variables, and ISO 8601 dates, mean your terms mean the same thing to everyone. Where
  no standard exists, define your terms explicitly.
- **Provenance.** Record where your inputs came from, what you did to them, and which version of the code produced
  the outputs.

Asking a colleague to follow your README without any help from you is a great final check.

## Two water repositories compared

| | **HydroShare** | **EDI** |
|---|---|---|
| **Run by** | CUAHSI | Environmental Data Initiative |
| **Best suited to** | Hydrologic data, models, code, notebooks, and teaching materials | Environmental data, including ecological and long-term monitoring data |
| **Metadata** | Web forms on the resource page, plus extra metadata for content types like time series, rasters, and NetCDF | Ecological Metadata Language (EML), created with tools like ezEML or EMLassemblyline |
| **Review before publishing** | Light review by CUAHSI staff for minimum metadata | Required automated evaluation of the metadata and its match to the data, with curators available for advice |
| **DOIs** | One DOI per published resource. A [new version](https://help.hydroshare.org/creating-and-managing-resources/creating-resource-versions) is a separate resource with its own identifier, linked to the previous version | Every version of a data package gets its own DOI and identifier |
| **Collaboration and compute** | Staged sharing with people and groups, linked JupyterHub environments, and the `hsclient` Python package | Primarily a publication and archive step |

HydroShare's strengths are collaboration before publication and keeping data, models, and code together with the
means to run them. The trade-off is that published content is locked, so you need to finish everything before
publishing. EDI's strengths are its structured, standardized metadata and built-in checks. The trade-off is that you
need to prepare that metadata in EML, which is an extra step if you haven't worked with it before.

### More on HydroShare

HydroShare has [guidance on its minimum metadata requirements](https://help.hydroshare.org/publishing-in-hydroshare/minimum-metadata-requirements-for-publishing-in-hydroshare/):
a descriptive title, an abstract, and at least three keywords including geographic ones. It shows what your
resource's DOI will be before you permanently publish, but the DOI only starts working once the resource is
published, so until then you cite the resource by its URL.
[Its recommended workflow](https://help.hydroshare.org/introduction-to-hydroshare/getting-started/permanently-publish-a-resource/):

1. Make the resource public when you submit the paper, and cite it by URL.
2. Switch to the DOI once the paper is accepted.
3. Add the paper's reference to the resource's related resources once the paper has its DOI.
4. Permanently publish the resource.

The paper and the resource then cite each other by DOI. If you would like help getting a dataset across the finish
line, CUAHSI runs the Data Publishing Program, a short virtual cohort offered twice a year that guides researchers
through publishing a dataset in HydroShare. See the
[Spring 2026 announcement](https://www.cuahsi.org/events/apply-for-the-cuahsi-data-publishing-program) for an example.

### EDI and other options

At the [Environmental Data Initiative (EDI)](https://edirepository.org), data are published as **data packages**,
which pair the data files with metadata written in Ecological Metadata Language (EML). Before a package can be
published, it must pass an [automated evaluation](https://edirepository.org/resources/evaluating-a-data-package)
that checks the metadata and its match with the data.

Other domain repositories may suit parts of your work. The [EarthChem Library](https://www.earthchem.org), for
example, curates geochemical data and works with SESAR, which registers physical samples with persistent IDs called
IGSNs. [AGU's list of domain repositories](https://data.agu.org/resources/useful-domain-repositories) and
[re3data](https://www.re3data.org) are good places to look further.

## Publishing derived data: two more checks

Beyond "snapshot or recipe", two more points from the checklist:

- **Avoid problematic duplication.** Mirroring entire archives is costly, goes stale, and splits citations. Make your
  derived product clearly distinct from the original in its title and description so that nobody mistakes it for the
  official dataset.
- **Plan for change.** Sources get updated and corrected, so record which version you used, and be ready to publish
  a new version of your product if the source changes in a meaningful way.

For example, imagine analyzing output from a national hydrologic model. The agency may only post its latest
operational output for a short window, while long historical simulations live in stable public archives. A subset of
the short-lived output is worth publishing as a snapshot; a subset of a stable archive may only need a pointer and
code. The USGS data release
[*National Water Model V1.2 Retrospective and Operational Model Run Archive for Selected NWIS Gage Locations*](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9ZRX948)
is a real-world example, where streamflow for about 18,000 gage locations was extracted from public model output and
reshaped to be quicker to read.

## Peer review of data and code

Peer review of data and code is less standardized than it is for papers, but there are several options, and they can
stand alone from a journal article:

- **Repository review.** The EarthChem Library's curators review metadata completeness and formatting but do not
  assess data quality, HydroShare staff do a light review for minimum metadata, and EDI requires its automated
  evaluation to pass. Others, like Zenodo, rely mostly on you, so a checklist and a colleague are a good idea.
- **Data journals.** A data paper is a short, peer-reviewed article that describes a dataset in detail while the data
  live in a repository. Examples include [Earth System Science Data](https://essd.copernicus.org),
  [Scientific Data](https://www.nature.com/sdata/), Data in Brief, and Geoscience Data Journal. ESSD, for example,
  requires the data to be in a
  [suitable repository](https://www.earth-system-science-data.net/policies/repository_criteria.html) with a DOI.
- **Software review.** The [Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)](https://joss.theoj.org) peer reviews research
  software, and [rOpenSci](https://ropensci.org) and [pyOpenSci](https://www.pyopensci.org) run community review of
  R and Python packages.
- **Review alongside a paper.** Use a private or temporary review link from the repository, ask what your journal
  prefers, or make the data public early.
- **Informal review.** Ask a colleague to open your data or run your code cold, and to answer five questions:
  1. Can they tell how the files relate to each other?
  2. Do they know where to start?
  3. Are the parameters described?
  4. Can they tell how the data were compiled?
  5. Is the code included?

## Key terms

- **Persistent identifier:** a permanent, unique label for a dataset, paper, person or organization that keeps
  working even if web pages move, such as a DOI or an ORCID iD.
- **Provenance:** the record of where data came from and what was done to them.
- **README:** a plain-text or Markdown file that introduces a project or dataset; often called its front page.
- **Replicability:** consistent results across studies that ask the same question, each with its own data.
